overview: Inuit history spans many regional communities across the Arctic. Archaeologists use Thule for the material culture of their ancestors, whose eastward migrations helped shape life in Arctic Canada. This map’s 1492 to 1500 window is a short snapshot, not the lifespan of Inuit peoples.

periods.title: Migration and regional settlement
periods.summary: Thule ancestors spread across Arctic Canada, with important regional differences in timing and settlement.

periods.title: Changing regional lives
periods.summary: Communities adapted their homes, travel and economies through environmental and social changes.

items.text: In the Auyuittuq region, early Thule winter houses used stone, sod and whale bones. A low entrance led into a partly sunken interior. Whale ribs could support a roof covered with skins and sod: a large animal supplied building material as well as food.

Inside these houses, a rear platform provided sleeping space, with storage beneath. Side platforms held oil lamps and supported cooking and drying clothing. Keeping clothes dry was household work with consequences far beyond looking tidy.

Skin boats and sleds connected camps. Parks Canada describes kayaks, larger umiaqs and dog transport among the Thule technologies used around Auyuittuq. Different seasons changed which routes were open and which animals people sought.

Western communities developed their own solutions. Around the Beaufort Sea, driftwood provided logs for houses with raised living floors, lowered entrances and sod coverings. A useful building material could arrive on the coast without a nearby forest.

Around the thirteenth century, Beaufort Sea communities developed net fishing and communal beluga hunts using kayaks. Such a hunt depended on several people coordinating their movements. The western history has its own pattern, rather than simply repeating Baffin Island’s story.

Making fitted skin clothing required small, precise tools. The Memorial University account describes piercing holes with a bone awl, then sewing with a fine bone needle. A needle was much smaller than a harpoon, but both mattered to living in the Arctic.

Thule finds include combs, needle cases and clothing fragments preserved in frozen deposits. These modest objects reveal grooming and repairs alongside hunting equipment. Archaeology can recover the work of maintaining a household, not only spectacular weapons.

A published collection from Cape Walker includes a wooden doll and a miniature scraper or ulu made of baleen. These actual small objects bring children and play into the archaeological picture. Their exact games are harder to recover than the toys themselves.

Parks Canada holds snow goggles dating to the mid-nineteenth century. Narrow eye slits reduced glare from snow and the risk of snow blindness. The specimen is later than this map snapshot, but records an ingenious protection that did not need glass lenses.

At Many Caches in the western Arctic, carefully fitted limestone slabs form vaulted storage places. Research combines archaeology with Inuvialuit knowledge of hunting. Two dated caribou bones establish later use; they do not date every cache or prove the entire site began at once.

The modern Tusaalanga lesson writes “ᖁᔭᓐᓇᒦᒃ”, transliterated “Qujannamiik”, for “Thank you”. This is an attested Inuktut teaching sample. Other dialects use different expressions, so it should not be treated as the only Inuit way to give thanks.

The writing systems came much later than 1492. ITK’s history records nineteenth-century missionary publications in syllabics and later Inuit-led standardization. In 2019 it adopted a shared Roman-alphabet orthography while communities continued using syllabics and other regional systems.

ending.text: There was no Inuit collapse in 1500. Inuit communities and languages continue, with their own organizations pursuing rights and self-determination. Colonial disruption and changing settlement patterns belong to the subsequent history; they do not turn a living people into an extinct civilization.
